interactions.label: A virus-infected hepatocyte displays viral peptides on its surface. Through whic

params.question: A virus-infected hepatocyte displays viral peptides on its surface. Through which pathway will the immune system specifically recognise and destroy this cell?

answers.text: Complement-mediated lysis via the membrane attack complex

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complement can lyse pathogens directly, but specific recognition and killing of a virus-infected nucleated cell requires the MHC class I pathway, which presents intracellular peptides to CD8-positive cytotoxic T cells.

answers.text: Natural killer cell recognition through the missing-self mechanism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: NK cells detect cells that have lost MHC class I expression entirely. When MHC class I is present and displaying viral peptides, the specific adaptive response via CD8-positive T cells is the primary killing pathway.

answers.text: CD8-positive cytotoxic T-cell recognition of viral peptides presented on MHC class I

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. All nucleated cells express MHC class I, which presents intracellular peptides — including viral proteins — to CD8-positive cytotoxic T cells for specific killing.

Neutrophil phagocytosis targets extracellular pathogens as part of innate immunity. Killing virus-infected nucleated cells requires the MHC class I to CD8-positive T-cell pathway of adaptive immunity.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the MHC class I pathway: all nucleated cells express MHC class I, which presents intracellular peptides to CD8-positive cytotoxic T cells. This is the specific adaptive mechanism for destroying virus-infected cells.
Well done. MHC class I on all nucleated cells presents endogenous peptides to CD8-positive cytotoxic T cells — this is how the adaptive immune system detects and eliminates intracellular infections.

interactions.label: A patient with glomerulonephritis has normal serum complement levels. Which hype

params.question: A patient with glomerulonephritis has normal serum complement levels. Which hypersensitivity mechanism is most consistent with this finding?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Type I hypersensitivity involves IgE and mast cells causing immediate reactions such as anaphylaxis and the atopic triad, not glomerulonephritis.

answers.text: Type II — antibodies directed against cell-surface antigens

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In Type II hypersensitivity (e.g., Goodpasture syndrome), antibodies bind directly to the glomerular basement membrane. Complement activates locally but is not consumed systemically, so serum C3 and C4 remain normal.

In Type III reactions (e.g., SLE nephritis), circulating immune complexes deposit in glomeruli and activate complement systemically. This consumes C3 and C4, causing low serum levels — the opposite of what is described here.
Type IV is purely cell-mediated with no antibody or complement involvement. It would not produce the antibody-mediated glomerulonephritis pattern described.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the key contrast: in Type II (e.g., Goodpasture), antibodies bind fixed tissue antigens locally, so serum complement stays normal. In Type III (e.g., SLE), circulating immune complexes consume complement systemically, causing low C3 and C4.

Excellent. The Goodpasture versus SLE comparison is a high-yield distinction: Type II targets antigens in situ with normal serum complement, while Type III deposits circulating complexes and consumes complement systemically.

interactions.label: Chronic transplant rejection can be reversed with immunosuppressive therapy such

params.question: Chronic transplant rejection can be reversed with immunosuppressive therapy such as calcineurin inhibitors and anti-thymocyte globulin.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. The narration explicitly states that chronic rejection has no effective treatment. It produces irreversible fibrosis and transplant arteriopathy. Immunosuppressants like calcineurin inhibitors and anti-thymocyte globulin are used for acute rejection only.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Chronic rejection causes progressive fibrosis and transplant arteriopathy over months to years, and no effective treatment exists. Calcineurin inhibitors and anti-thymocyte globulin are effective against acute rejection, not chronic.

params.question: In a patient with active SLE, serum C3 and C4 levels are markedly low while anti-double-stranded DNA titres are rising. Which sequence of events best explains these simultaneous findings?

answers.text: Anti-dsDNA antibodies directly inhibit hepatic synthesis of complement components

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complement levels in SLE flares fall because of consumption, not reduced synthesis. Immune complexes activate and deplete complement faster than the liver can replenish it.

answers.text: Anti-dsDNA antibodies form immune complexes with nuclear antigens; these complexes deposit in tissues and activate the classical complement pathway, consuming C3 and C4

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Rising anti-dsDNA titres generate more immune complexes with persistent nuclear debris. These deposit in glomeruli and vessels, activating complement via the classical pathway and consuming C3 and C4 systemically — which is why complement levels inversely track disease activity.

answers.text: Regulatory T-cell dysfunction releases complement-activating cytokines into the circulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While regulatory T-cell loss contributes to autoimmunity in SLE, complement consumption is driven by immune complex deposition and classical pathway activation, not by a cytokine-mediated mechanism.

answers.text: Low complement reflects a genetic C1q deficiency that predisposes to SLE, independent of disease activity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: C1q deficiency does predispose to SLE by impairing apoptotic debris clearance, but falling C3 and C4 during a flare reflect active consumption by immune complexes. Complement levels rise again when the flare subsides, confirming this is activity-driven, not static.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key chain is: anti-dsDNA antibodies + nuclear antigens → immune complexes → tissue deposition → classical complement activation → C3 and C4 consumption. Falling complement with rising anti-dsDNA together signal an active SLE flare.

Well done. In SLE, anti-dsDNA titres and complement levels move in opposite directions during flares — rising autoantibodies form more immune complexes, which consume complement. This inverse relationship is used clinically to monitor disease activity.

interactions.label: In HIV infection, a clinician monitors both CD4 count and viral load. Which stat

params.question: In HIV infection, a clinician monitors both CD4 count and viral load. Which statement best explains how these two markers differ in their clinical utility?

answers.text: CD4 count predicts the speed of disease progression; viral load indicates current immune function

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reverses the roles. The CD4 count shows where the patient currently stands immunologically, while the viral load set point predicts how rapidly the disease will progress toward AIDS.

answers.text: Both markers reflect the same aspect of disease and are clinically interchangeable

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These markers provide complementary but distinct information. Two patients with the same CD4 count but different viral load set points will progress at very different rates.

answers.text: CD4 count indicates the patient's current immune status; the viral load set point predicts the rate of disease progression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The CD4 count tells you where the patient is — their current level of immunosuppression — while the viral load set point tells you how fast they are travelling toward AIDS. The set point is the strongest predictor of progression speed.

answers.text: Viral load is relevant only after AIDS is diagnosed; CD4 count is the sole monitoring marker during clinical latency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Viral load is essential during all phases. During clinical latency, a high set point predicts rapid CD4 decline, guiding decisions about when to initiate antiretroviral therapy.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the key distinction: CD4 count = current immune status (where the patient is now). Viral load set point = rate of progression (how fast they are moving toward AIDS). These two markers are complementary, not interchangeable.
Exactly right. 'The CD4 count tells you where the patient is; viral load tells you how fast they are travelling.' This principle guides clinical monitoring throughout HIV infection.
